passages: [prose] The study was conducted at CDNP, situated 5.5 km east of Darwin (12°27′S, 130°50′E) in the NT, Australia. The park vegetation is representative of typical northern Australian tropical savanna woodland. Eucalyptus tetrodonta and E. miniata dominate the overstorey, over a patchy understorey of annual and perennial grasses. The park is of natural and cultural significance, protecting part of the nationally significant Port Darwin wetland (48 km 2 ). The climate is wet-dry tropical and characterised by high temperatures throughout the year. Mean daily maximum and minimum temperatures are 31.9°C and 23.2°C, respectively (Bureau of Meteorology, NT). Mean annual rainfall is \~1700 mm, with over 90% falling during the wet season (November to April).

Of the 24 baits installed, 50% were attacked after 2.5 months. Stakes (58%) and paper (42%) baits were attacked at similar frequency.

[prose] No single species dominated baits. The frequency of occurrence of four species (S. actuosus, M. boreus, H. vagus and H. venustus) was similar, ranging from 19% to 25% of total bait observations (Table 1). These species attacked both bait types and were recorded in both sites. For both sites, 50% of the baits installed were attacked by week 10.

The lack of repeated/ seasonal sampling and the fewer sites surveyed may contribute to the observed difference. Fourteen of the 16 species sampled in the present study were recorded in Kakadu savanna woodland by Braithwaite et al. (1988). The three most abundant species in the present study (N. eucalypti, S. actuosus and M. boreus) were also among the most common species encountered by Braithwaite et al. (1988). However, in the later study M. darwiniensis was more common and the grass harvester Amitermes laurensis was the most frequent species sampled.

[prose] The results of the current study only partially support the a priori predictions for termite feeding groups at CDNP, based on the work of Braithwaite et al. (1988). Wood and soil feeders were the dominant feeding groups in Kakadu savanna woodland, and grass-harvesting species were common (Braithwaite et al. 1988). In the present study wood feeders were dominant, but wood/soil interface feeders were also common. As predicted from Braithwaite et al.’s findings (1988), species from the wood-feeding genera Mastotermes, Coptotermes, Schedorhinotermes and Microcerotermes were also present at CDNP. The wood/soil interface feeder N. eucalypti dominated the CDNP termite fauna, followed by the dead wood feeders S. actuosus and M. boreus. Casual observations of termite communities around Darwin also support the dominance of wood and wood/soil-feeding termite species in savanna woodland (Dawes-Gromadzki & Spain 2003; G Ragno unpubl. data 2003; Dawes-Gromadzki 2005a).

[prose] Four nesting habits were represented, with 88% of species nesting either in epigeal mounds or below ground (Fig. 4). Epigeal-nesting species included N. eucalypti, Nasutitermes longipennis, Microcerotermes spp., C. acinaciformis, Ephelotermes spp., Macrognathotermes spp. and A. perelegans (Table 1).

[prose] A number of soil characteristics can also influence termite species diversity and abundance (Lee & Wood 1971; Jones & Prasetyo 2002; Dawes-Gromadzki 2005a). Soils with poor drainage capacity or inundation susceptibility can inhibit activity and provide unsuitable conditions for soil-dwelling and mound-building species (Jones 2000; Dawes-Gromadzki 2005a). In such environments, wood- and arboreal-nesting species are common. The dominance of mound- and soildwelling species in the present study is consistent with the elevated, well-draining kandosol soils of CDNP. However, although the species diversity observed is greater than that observed for seasonally inundated monsoon forest sites nearby (Dawes-Gromadzki 2005a), the relatively lower species diversity compared with Kakadu woodland may relate to soil fertility. In contrast to studies from tropical African and Indonesian rainforests (Dibog et al. 1999; Jones & Prasetyo 2002), Braithwaite et al. (1988) found a negative relationship between soil fertility and termite species richness. Compared with Kakadu, CDNP soils may be of generally lower fertility. At some sites soil depth appeared shallow, with patches of exposed rocky ground. This was particularly evident at site 4, which recorded the lowest species number. Patchiness in ground vegetation may also explain the lower species diversity (Braithwaite et al. 1988).

[prose] The termite nesting habits documented at CDNP did support the a priori predictions based on the work of Braithwaite et al. (1988). At CDNP epigeal- and hypogeal-nesting species were dominant. Epigeal-nesting species were the most common followed by hypogeal-nesting species, supported by the high termite encounter rates in mounds and lying dead wood, respectively. In Kakadu, epigeal- and hypogeal-nesting species were also dominant. Wood- and arboreal-nesting species were also scarce, as in the present study. For the epigeal nesters, Braithwaite et al. (1988) also recorded species that inhabit the mounds of other termites, including A. perelegans.
